quality_rules.zut_note: Same English intention must always produce the same PA Dutch target. Multiple English phrasings may legitimately converge on one PA Dutch form (e.g. 'think that' and 'think about' both → denke) — that convergence is fine and expected; it is the reverse-direction flexibility ZUT allows.

phrase_tips: Keep clause-final verb placement correct even in short BUILD fragments — don't default to English SVO order.
Prefer the modals (will/kann/muss) over periphrastic alternatives while the paradigm is still being seeded.
vocabulary_constraints: Only 1st person singular available at seed 1 — full modal paradigm (witt/welle) doesn't fill in until 2nd/3rd person subjects are introduced (~seed 13-20).
Progressive 'am + infinitive' construction should be introduced early (it recurs constantly) but only after 'bin'/'bischt' (am/are) exist.
Negation 'net' should be front-loaded — it's a structural cliff, not a late-course refinement.

methodology_insights: PA Dutch is NOT Standard Hochdeutsch — resist the temptation to 'correct' toward Hochdeutsch forms (e.g. 'sprechen' is never used; the settled PA Dutch verb is 'schwetze'). When in doubt, prefer the form already established by the existing 300-seed translation set over a more 'proper' German-looking alternative.

The existing Pass-1 translations (seeds 1-300) are already consistent and idiomatic — reuse their established vocabulary/forms (schwetze, browiere, gleiche, kenne/wisse split, waer-future, am-progressive) rather than re-deriving alternate translations during LEGO decomposition.

Modal conjugation (will/witt/will/welle/welle/welle) must be taught as a paradigm across seeds via person — don't atomize 'will' alone and then silently swap to 'witt' for 2nd person without a dedicated LEGO/overlap step.

Subordinate-clause verb-final order after as/wann/weil/eb is a recurring structural mismatch vs English — always M-LEGO the connector + clause together rather than atomizing the connector alone, so the word-order shift is taught in-context.
opus_polish_guidance: Priority: keep English known_text natural and conversational — never stilted just to make PA Dutch tiling easier.
Flag any PA Dutch phrase that looks like a literal Hochdeutsch calque instead of settled PA Dutch usage.
Preserve the wisse/kennen and sehne/scheine splits established in Pass 1 — don't let later seeds blur them.

known_language_guidance.trust_test: Would a native English speaker say this naturally?
known_language_guidance.quality_bar: Natural, idiomatic English — the learner knows this language and full sentences must read like something a person would actually say.

avoid_patterns.reason: known side must stay in the learner's own language
avoid_patterns.use_instead: keep spelled out in known_text (canonical uses {target} substitution) — never abbreviate to 'PA Dutch' or 'Deitsch' in the known column

register_notes: Casual, everyday register throughout — matches the informal 'du' register on the target side.
No formal/polite English register needed since PA Dutch has no T/V split to mirror.

target_language_guidance.quality_bar: Correct, natural PA Dutch (Deitsch) as actually spoken by Pennsylvania Dutch/Amish-Mennonite communities — closely related to Palatine German (Pfälzisch) but with its own settled orthography and English loan influence. Can have pedagogical structure, but must never be invented/Hochdeutsch-calqued where PA Dutch has its own settled form.

common_patterns.target_form: am + infinitive (+ sei for stative be)

structural_notes: Verb-second (V2) main-clause word order, like German: finite verb in position 2 of a statement (Ich will nau schwetze), subject-verb inversion for questions and after a fronted adverbial (Fer was bischt du...).

Modal + infinitive: modals (will/witt/welle 'want', kann/kannscht/kenne 'can', muss/musscht/misse 'must', soll 'should') take a BARE infinitive at clause end — no linking particle, unlike English 'to'.

Non-modal verb + infinitive DOES take a linking particle: 'browiere zu' (try to), 'fer' + infinitive after adjectives/nouns of purpose ('reddi fer geh' = ready to go, 'Zeit fer schwetze' = time to speak). Don't confuse modal (bare) vs non-modal (zu/fer) infinitive constructions.

Subordinate clauses (after 'as' [that], 'wann' [if/when], 'weil' [because], 'eb' [whether]) push the finite verb to clause-final position, exactly like German subclauses — this is a hard, always-on word-order shift, not optional.

Present perfect (haben/sei + past participle) is the default PAST TENSE in speech — PA Dutch, like colloquial German, has essentially no simple past for most verbs. 'wanted to' = 'hab...welle', 'wrote' = 'hot...geschriwwe'.

Personal pronoun + verb contraction is extremely common and often mandatory in speech: bischt du → bischt-du is written separately but pronounced fused; 'hoscht du' (have you), 'witt du' (do you want) are the normal question forms via subject-verb inversion, not a periphrastic do-support.
No do-support: questions and negation are formed by inversion (Schwetzscht du...?) and the negator 'net' placed after the finite verb / before the negated element — never an auxiliary 'do'.

Definite/indefinite articles (der/die/es, en) still carry grammatical gender (masc/fem/neut) like German, though case marking is heavily reduced (nominative/accusative merged for most contexts in casual speech; dative survives mainly in pronouns like 'mir', 'dir', 'ihm').

Progressive/continuous aspect is formed periphrastically with 'am' + infinitive (+ optional 'sei'): 'am lanne' (learning), 'bin am duh' (am doing) — PA Dutch has a true grammaticalised progressive, unlike Standard German.

register.rationale: Pennsylvania Dutch has no functional T/V distinction in everyday speech (unlike Standard German's du/Sie split) — Amish/Mennonite and PA Dutch speech communities use 'du' universally regardless of the addressee's status. The whole course uses 'du' consistently; a formal register was never introduced.

target_forms.trigger: know a fact / know how to do something / know that X
know a person / be acquainted with someone or somewhere

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: 'know [fact/how-to]' = wisse (e.g. 'wisse wie mer sell dutt'); 'know [person/place]' = kenne (e.g. 'kenn selli Leit'). Mirrors the German wissen/kennen split.

target_forms.trigger: we/they want — plural present, and the bare infinitive after another finite verb

target_forms.target: hab ... welle / hot ... welle / hen ... welle
target_forms.trigger: wanted (past) — periphrastic perfect, PA Dutch has no simple past for this verb

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: 'want' is a modal verb (like German wollen) inflected by person/number: will/witt/will/welle/welle/welle. Past 'wanted to' is always the present-perfect periphrasis (haben + welle), never a simple past form — PA Dutch productive verbs use the perfect for narrative past.

target_forms.trigger: be going to V — near-future intention, 1st/2nd/3rd person of the 'waer(e)' future auxiliary + bare infinitive

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: 'going to V' = waer + infinitive (not geh + infinitive, which is reserved for literal physical 'go'). Distinguish from literal motion 'go' = geh.

target_forms.trigger: seem like / look as if (impersonal 'it seems')

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: 'see' (visual) = sehne; 'seem' (appear) = scheine or 'es guckt as wann'. Never conflate — different verbs, unrelated to the 'see' family in English.

target_forms.trigger: remember / recall — always reflexive, uni-directional; PA Dutch does not split retain-vs-recall the way Japanese does

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: Single consistent reflexive verb 'sich erinnere' (an + acc. or uff + acc.) covers all 'remember' senses in this course — no fork needed.

target_forms.trigger: think that X (opinion) / think about X (deliberate) — single verb covers both

problem_verbs.disambiguation_rule: 'denke' is used for both 'think that' and 'think about' — PA Dutch does not lexically split these the way some languages do. Kept as one form to avoid a false ZUT fork.
